packs.title: Stone Keeps Stories
packs.promise: Read Rome through small shapes, quiet gestures and a crossing of your own.

q.s: Find the shapes between the Pantheon’s solid forms.
st: From the public square, look toward the Pantheon’s columned portico without joining the entrance queue.
Find a tall rectangle between columns, a triangle near the roof, and a patch of sky shaped by the building edge.
Record which empty shape seems lightest and which seems most solid. There is no correct answer.
Save your three shapes and the comparison in a field note or photo caption.

q.s: Compose a quiet rhythm from the hill’s repeating lines.
st: Stay at a comfortable public viewpoint near Piazza d’Aracoeli and look toward the broad Cordonata leading uphill. You do not need to climb.
Choose three repeating visual beats: a step edge, a vertical support, and a change in shadow.
Arrange the beats into a short rhythm written as words, dots, or dashes. Keep it silent and let unequal spacing count.
Give the rhythm a short title and save it as a note or a photograph with a caption.

q.s: Carry one detail across the Tiber and give it a partner.
st: At the Via dei Pettinari end of Ponte Sisto, choose an open pedestrian route and one detail of the riverbank to remember.
Cross at a comfortable pace without stopping in a bottleneck. At the Piazza Trilussa end, choose one different detail from the new side.
Write one sentence joining the two observations with the word “and.” A shorter out-and-back or a stationary pair of views works too.
Save both details and the joining sentence.

packs.title: Clay and Steel
packs.promise: Read Testaccio and Ostiense through containers, old walls and industrial forms.

q.s: Turn a marble pyramid into a compact shape study.
st: Use an open public sidewalk view outside the monument fence. Find the pyramid’s point and the two sloping edges visible from your position.
Draw those edges and a base line as a small shape, or describe their relationship. Make a second version by changing just one slope.
Compare the versions in one sentence. Your changed shape is a design experiment, not a measurement of the tomb.

q.s: Plan a short exterior loop around a neighbourhood market.
st: From an open public sidewalk, identify the modern covered market building. Use a current street map to locate Via Alessandro Volta and Via Lorenzo Ghiberti around it.
Plan an exterior walking loop using public sidewalks and marked crossings. Mark your start, a corner where direction changes and the return; keep doors and loading areas clear.
Walk as much of the loop as suits you, or trace it on the map from a comfortable place. Record one detail of the market’s roof or entrances without needing an open stall.

q.s: Compare an ancient sculpture detail with industrial machinery.
st: For an in-person museum visit, check current opening and admission, including any eligibility for free entry. Allow admission and queue time separately. The free source-image version earns the same credit.
In the machine hall or linked museum images, choose one visible machine component and one ancient sculpture detail. Write a short description of the shape or material of each; do not touch displays.

Pause for about a minute in an open visitor position or with the official images. Place the two descriptions beside each other and note one contrast between them, then a word for the pace you want to carry onward. A photograph inside the museum is unnecessary.
